nodes.label: generic-runner HelmRelease (ARC scale set base)
nodes.rationale: Single placeholder-valued gha-runner-scale-set HelmRelease acts as the shared template for every repo/org runner overlay; githubConfigUrl and githubConfigSecret are deliberately 'placeholder' so each overlay must JSON-patch them, making an unpatched overlay fail loudly rather than register against the wrong account. containerMode kubernetes with a longhorn-local RWO work PVC keeps job workspaces node-local.

nodes.label: david-driscoll-runners overlay
nodes.rationale: Registered repo-scoped against github.com/david-driscoll/crew, NOT account-scoped: david-driscoll is a User account, not an org, so a bare account URL makes ARC call /orgs/david-driscoll/... which 404s and crash-loops the listener. Personal accounts only support repo-level runners — one scale set per repo, which is why ./vault exists as a sibling instead of one shared account scale set. minRunners 0 / maxRunners 2 keeps an idle-scale-to-zero footprint.

nodes.label: littles-tech-runners overlay
nodes.rationale: Org-scoped (github.com/littlestechnology) so one scale set serves every repo in the org — the opposite of the personal-account overlays. It is the heavy tier: minRunners 1 keeps a warm runner, maxRunners 4, and it is the only overlay that add-patches container resources up to 2 CPU / 3Gi request and 8Gi limit for build-heavy jobs.

nodes.label: littles-tech-release Flux Kustomization
nodes.rationale: Uniquely dependsOn the sibling littles-tech Kustomization rather than gha-repositories, because it reuses the littles-tech-github-app secret that the littles-tech overlay provisions via its own ./secret.yaml — applying release first would leave the HelmRelease pointing at a missing secret.

nodes.label: littles-tech-release-runners overlay
nodes.rationale: The only overlay with no ./secret.yaml of its own — it borrows littles-tech-github-app from the sibling littles-tech overlay. Separate scale set (max 3, min 1) so release workflows get a dedicated queue that PR/CI load cannot starve.

nodes.label: vault-runners overlay
nodes.rationale: Repo-scoped against github.com/david-driscoll/vault for the same User-account-is-not-an-org reason as the david-driscoll overlay. vault is the crew's private issue tracker and the only repo whose workflows need a runner: crew-claude.yml executes here and checks out the other estate repos via an app token, so this one scale set is the entry point for all crew automation.

nodes.label: onepassword-connect HelmRelease
nodes.rationale: Tier 0 component: OpenBao cannot boot at exit without external-secrets + onepassword-connect, so both pods must remain schedulable on a control plane once the low-power tier's control-plane taint is live (docs/cluster-consolidation/20-low-power-tier.md §4). connect.tolerations and operator.tolerations are SEPARATE chart keys — setting only one silently leaves the other pod untolerated, so both are set. Reloader annotations on the deployment and service force a restart when the credentials secret or access token rotates.

nodes.label: onepassword-connect HTTPRoute (disabled)
nodes.rationale: A Gateway API HTTPRoute onto the network/internal Gateway that would expose op-connect.${CLUSTER_DOMAIN} to port 8080, but it is commented out of kustomization.yaml — the chart's own Traefik ingress (ingressClassName internal) currently owns that hostname instead. Kept in-tree as the migration target rather than deleted.

nodes.label: onepassword-connect Flux Kustomization
nodes.rationale: Supplies APP and NAMESPACE via postBuild.substitute, which is what lets uptime.yaml name itself ${APP} and stay generic. wait: true because downstream ExternalSecret stores cannot reconcile until Connect is actually serving.

nodes.label: 1Password Connect ApplicationDefinition
nodes.rationale: Custom driscoll.dev/v1 ApplicationDefinition CR that declares the Gatus health probe (https://op-connect.${CLUSTER_DOMAIN}/health expecting 200) and the admins-only access policy in one place, so monitoring and authz are derived from the app manifest rather than hand-maintained in a central Gatus config.

nodes.label: Cilium Hubble ApplicationDefinition (commented out)
nodes.rationale: Entirely commented out, yet still listed in kustomization.yaml resources — it renders to nothing today. It preserves the intended shape of Hubble exposure: an Authentik forward_single proxy in front of hubble.${CLUSTER_DOMAIN} with an admins-only policy and a matching Gatus check, ready to re-enable.

nodes.label: cilium HelmRelease
nodes.rationale: Carries no inline values at all: everything comes from valuesFrom the cilium-values ConfigMap, which the sibling kustomization.yaml generates from ./helm/values.yaml. That indirection keeps the CNI config a plain YAML file (editable/lintable) while still getting Kustomize's hash-suffixed ConfigMap regeneration on change.

nodes.label: cilium HelmRepository
nodes.rationale: Deliberately declared in kube-system rather than flux-system — the inline comment states the namespace is required for Renovate lookups to resolve the chart version.

nodes.label: cilium Flux Kustomization
nodes.rationale: deletionPolicy: Orphan so the CNI is never cascade-deleted merely because ownership of the Kustomization changes (e.g. a namespace-redirect flip during consolidation) — see docs/cluster-consolidation/27-migration-churn-failure-modes.md. wait: false because Cilium's own readiness would deadlock a health check that depends on cluster networking already working.

nodes.label: cilium Kustomization (values ConfigMap generator)
nodes.rationale: configMapGenerator turns ./helm/values.yaml into the cilium-values ConfigMap, and ./helm/kustomizeconfig.yaml teaches Kustomize to rewrite the hashed name into the HelmRelease's valuesFrom reference — without that configurations entry the HelmRelease would point at a stale, non-existent ConfigMap name.

nodes.label: CiliumL2AnnouncementPolicy l2-policy
nodes.rationale: ARP-announces the pool's LoadBalancer IPs on Linux nodes. The interface regexes (ens*, enp*s*, eth*) exist because a host with more than one active NIC would otherwise announce on the wrong link; this is the L2 (no BGP) path to service reachability.

nodes.label: CiliumLoadBalancerIPPool pool
nodes.rationale: Two blocks (.100-.200 and .202-.252) inside ${LOADBALANCER_RANGE} with a deliberate gap at .201, reserving that address for something outside Cilium's allocator. allowFirstLastIPs: No keeps network/broadcast addresses out of the pool.

nodes.label: gha-arc-controller (ARC controller dependency)
nodes.rationale: Every runner scale set both dependsOn the controller HelmRelease and names its service account (gha-arc-controller/github-actions) in values.controllerServiceAccount, so the controller is a hard ordering and RBAC prerequisite for all four overlays.

nodes.label: ApplicationDefinition (driscoll.dev/v1) convention
nodes.rationale: Estate-local CRD (schema at schemas/definition.schema.json) that colocates dashboard icon/category, Authentik access policy, and Gatus checks with the app that owns them. Instances template on ${APP}, ${CLUSTER_TITLE} and ${CLUSTER_DOMAIN} so the same file works per-cluster.

nodes.label: Repo-scoped ARC registration for personal accounts
nodes.norm_label: repo-scoped arc registration for personal accounts
nodes.rationale: GitHub User accounts have no /orgs/<name> endpoint, so ARC's listener 404s and crash-loops if given a bare account githubConfigUrl. The estate therefore pays a one-scale-set-per-repo cost for david-driscoll/crew and david-driscoll/vault, while littlestechnology (a real org) gets a single account-scoped scale set covering all its repos.

nodes.label: Middleware: strip-query-string
nodes.rationale: Uses the traefik-plugin-query-modification plugin with paramNameRegex '.*' to delete every query parameter, so backends that leak or choke on query strings receive a clean URL.

nodes.label: Middleware: tailscale-network
nodes.rationale: ipAllowList pinned to the CGNAT range 100.64.0.0/10, which is the tailnet address space — this is the network-layer gate that restricts a route to tailnet clients only.

nodes.label: Middleware: tailscale-redirect
nodes.rationale: Currently a no-op empty chain; the redirectRegex that would rewrite hosts to the TAILSCALE_DOMAIN is commented out, so the resource exists as a stable alias slot that routes can reference without being redirected.

nodes.label: Middleware: tailscale-user
nodes.rationale: Composite chain layering error-pages, the authentik outpost, and tailscale-network so a route gets identity-based auth AND tailnet-only source filtering from a single ExtensionRef.

nodes.label: HelmRelease: csi-driver-nfs
nodes.rationale: Storage-driver release hardened for churn: 7 install/upgrade retries with rollback strategy, CRDs CreateReplace, recreate on rollback — a CSI driver that fails to converge takes every PVC in the cluster with it.

nodes.label: HelmRepository: csi-driver-nfs
nodes.rationale: Points straight at the upstream kubernetes-csi GitHub raw charts directory rather than an OCI mirror, unlike the observability apps in this repo which use ghcr.io charts-mirror OCIRepositories.

nodes.label: Flux Kustomization: csi-driver-nfs
nodes.rationale: wait: true because downstream PVC-consuming apps must not reconcile before the NFS driver is healthy; depends on onepassword-connect and external-secrets so the SPIKE_IP substitution chain is available.

nodes.label: ConfigMap generator: csi-driver-nfs-values
nodes.rationale: disableNameSuffixHash: true so the HelmRelease can reference a stable ConfigMap name in valuesFrom; the tradeoff is that values changes do not roll the release by name change alone.

nodes.label: StorageClass: nfs-csi
nodes.rationale: reclaimPolicy Retain protects the /mnt/stash share from PVC deletion; NFS 4.2 with nconnect=8 and hard mounts trades hung-on-outage behaviour for throughput and no silent I/O errors. Server address comes from the ${SPIKE_IP} substitution.

nodes.label: csi-driver-nfs chart values
nodes.rationale: mountPermissions 0 defers permission control to the NFS export; the controller disables its own snapshotter but enables externalSnapshotter, so snapshot CRs are served by the shared external component rather than a per-driver sidecar.

nodes.label: nfs-system namespace kustomization
nodes.rationale: pod-security enforce: privileged is required because CSI node plugins mount host paths and run privileged; pulls in the shared alerts and common components for every app in the namespace.

nodes.label: AlertmanagerConfig: alertmanager
nodes.rationale: Routes everything to pushover except severity=none and the InfoInhibitor/Watchdog alertnames which are black-holed to the 'null' receiver; a critical alert inhibits the matching warning on the same alertname+namespace to prevent double-paging.

nodes.label: Pushover receiver
nodes.rationale: Notification body falls back description -> summary -> message -> literal placeholder so an alert missing annotations still produces a readable page; credentials are pulled from the alertmanager-secret keys pushover_api_token and pushover_user_key.

nodes.label: ApplicationDefinition: alertmanager
nodes.rationale: Repo-local driscoll.dev/v1 CRD that drives three downstream systems from one place: authentik forward_single proxy provider, Gatus health check, and the dashboard entry. skipPathRegex ^/api exempts the API from the auth proxy so machine clients still work.

nodes.label: HelmRelease: alertmanager
nodes.rationale: Deploys the kube-prometheus-stack chart with every subchart disabled except alertmanager, so Alertmanager gets its own release lifecycle independent of Prometheus. driftDetection enabled and install retries -1 (retry forever).

nodes.label: Flux Kustomization: alertmanager
nodes.rationale: deletionPolicy Orphan per docs/cluster-consolidation/27-migration-churn-failure-modes.md so a Kustomization removal during migration churn cannot delete the live Alertmanager and its PVC; wait: false keeps it from blocking the observability chain.

nodes.label: alertmanager chart values
nodes.rationale: Control-plane toleration is documented in-file as placement flexibility ONLY: Alertmanager is a StatefulSet on a 1Gi Longhorn PVC, so a toleration widens where it MAY schedule but the pod still follows its volume. Exposed twice — Gateway API HTTPRoute behind the authenticated-user Traefik middleware, and a Tailscale service via tailscale.com/expose on the tailnet-outbound proxy-group.

nodes.label: ApplicationDefinition: alloy
nodes.rationale: Per-cluster app: category and URL are built from ${CLUSTER_TITLE}/${CLUSTER_DOMAIN} rather than the estate-wide ${ROOT_DOMAIN}, because alloy is a DaemonSet collector that exists once per cluster. The description text is copy-pasted from the alertmanager definition and does not describe alloy.

nodes.label: HelmRelease: alloy
nodes.rationale: configMap.create false + external alloy-configmap so the River config is version-controlled in resources/config.alloy; reloader auto annotation rolls the DaemonSet on config change. Control-plane toleration is justified in-file: alloy scrapes the node it runs on, so a control plane without it is an observability blind spot. Opens OTLP gRPC 4317 and HTTP 4318 as extra ports.

nodes.label: OCIRepository: alloy
nodes.rationale: Chart 1.12.0 pinned by sha256 digest as well as tag, pulled from the ghcr.io/home-operations/charts-mirror rather than upstream, so a republished tag cannot silently change the deployed chart.

nodes.label: Flux Kustomization: alloy
nodes.rationale: Same deletionPolicy Orphan migration-churn guard as alertmanager, but with wait: true and no dependsOn — alloy has no secret or repository prerequisites.

nodes.label: ConfigMap generator: alloy-configmap
nodes.rationale: Generates key config.alloy from ./resources/config.alloy with disableNameSuffixHash so the HelmRelease can name it statically; the reloader annotation on the controller is what actually propagates changes.

nodes.rationale: The folder that is actually deployed: kubernetes.yaml is in the dashboards kustomization resources list, k8s.yaml is not.

nodes.label: RoleBinding this-sa
nodes.rationale: Binds the namespace-local `this-sa` ServiceAccount to the cluster-wide kubernetes-external-secrets ClusterRole, giving the per-namespace SecretStore an identity to authenticate with. The YAML anchor `&name`/`*name` keeps the RoleBinding subject and the ServiceAccount name in sync.

nodes.label: Ingress ${APP}-tailscale-ingress
nodes.rationale: Exposes an app on the tailnet through the shared `tailnet-outbound` ProxyGroup rather than a per-app proxy, tagged tag:apps. Every knob is a defaulted substitution (TAILSCALE_SERVICE, TAILSCALE_PORT, TAILSCALE_HOST all fall back to ${APP}) so the common case needs no configuration at all. experimental-forward-cluster-traffic-via-ingress is required for the proxy to reach in-cluster backends.

nodes.label: tailscale Component
nodes.rationale: Stamps app.kubernetes.io/name and driscoll.dev/name commonLabels from ${APP} onto everything it renders, matching the labelling convention the volsync and postgres components use.

nodes.label: ExternalSecret ${APP}-volsync
nodes.rationale: Templates the restic repository credential Secret ${APP}-volsync-secret from the openbao ClusterSecretStore at apps/volsync/password (formerly the 1Password item 'Volsync Password' in vault Eris). RESTIC_REPOSITORY is derived per app as /repository/${APP} inside the shared mount, so each app gets its own restic repository. Carries reloader.stakater.com/auto so movers pick up a rotated password.

nodes.label: volsync Component
nodes.rationale: Bundles the four objects that make up an app's backup and restore path and stamps app.kubernetes.io/name, driscoll.dev/name and kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/force: enabled as commonLabels on all of them.

nodes.label: PersistentVolumeClaim ${APP}
nodes.rationale: The app's real data volume, provisioned through the VolSync volume populator via dataSourceRef -> ReplicationDestination/${APP}-dst so a first deploy restores from the latest restic snapshot instead of starting empty. Storage class is VOLSYNC_STORAGECLASS (default longhorn) — deliberately distinct from the mover's staging class since 2026-08-19.

nodes.label: ReplicationDestination ${APP}-dst
nodes.rationale: Restores the app's latest restic snapshot into a staging volume ${APP}-dst-dest that the app PVC then clones from. Uses its own VOLSYNC_STAGING_STORAGECLASS so restore churn can stay off a pinned tier. Cache default is 8Gi here versus 2Gi on the source — the asymmetry is why VOLSYNC_CACHE_CAPACITY should be pinned explicitly rather than inherited.

nodes.label: ReplicationSource ${APP}
nodes.rationale: Nightly (0 14 * * *) restic backup of the app PVC via a Snapshot copyMethod staging clone, retaining 7 daily / 4 weekly / 4 monthly / 1 yearly / last 5, pruning every 14 days. The staging clone gets its own VOLSYNC_STAGING_STORAGECLASS so an app can pin its data to one tier while disposable backup churn stays on another.

nodes.label: volsync component contract
nodes.rationale: The component provides the steady-state backup path: the ExternalSecret holding the restic repository credential, the nightly ReplicationSource, the app's PVC, and (since 639a049d) the ReplicationDestination. Consumers are Flux Kustomization CRs in the cluster repos referencing ../kubernetes/components/volsync via GitRepository/home-operations, so the references are invisible to a git grep inside this repo — search the cluster repos or query the live cluster before assuming a component is unused.

nodes.label: VOLSYNC_CAPACITY only ever goes up
nodes.rationale: Two one-way constraints fire together. resources.requests.storage is immutable downward, and with the kustomize force: enabled stamp Flux resolves the rejected patch by deleting the bound PVC and creating a new one. The replacement then cannot bind, because a snapshot cannot be restored into a volume smaller than its RESTORESIZE — still the old larger capacity. The symptom names neither cause: the app PVC and a vs-prime-* PVC both sit Pending forever with only 'assuming an external populator will provision the volume'. Recovery is to put the number back. Shipped once: #1084 cut forgejo 20Gi to 10Gi, Flux deleted the bound PVC within the minute, #1100 put it back; data loss was nil only because the forge's real state was in Postgres.

nodes.label: First-deploy volume populator trap
nodes.rationale: dataSourceRef is consulted only when a PVC is first created and is immutable and inert once Bound. On a brand-new PVC the VolSync populator claims it, Longhorn stands down ('assuming an external populator will provision the volume'), and the populator waits forever for a ReplicationDestination nothing creates — PVC Pending, no Longhorn volume, no obvious error (equestria-cluster#2987, stargate-command-cluster#1739). Shipping the destination unconditionally is what lets a first deploy or a forced PVC recreate bind on its own. Do not try to fix a stuck PVC by editing pvc.yaml: dataSourceRef is immutable and the populator re-enqueues unbound PVCs, so creating the ReplicationDestination is sufficient.

nodes.label: kustomize force: enabled stamp hazard
nodes.rationale: kustomization.yaml stamps kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/force: enabled on every resource in the component, so changing an immutable PVC field (storageClassName, dataSourceRef, or lowering requests.storage) makes Flux delete and recreate the PVC, destroying the data. Expanding VOLSYNC_CAPACITY is safe; changing storage class or lowering capacity is not.

nodes.label: Nightly destination rebuild cycle
nodes.rationale: spec.trigger.manual: restore-once fires once per destination; the volsync-restore-cleanup CronJob (30 3 * * *) deletes every destination whose status.lastManualSync caught up, cascading to its ${APP}-dst-dest/${APP}-dst-cache pair. Because the destination is declared in the component, Flux recreates it and the restore runs again — so every app performs a real restic restore at ~04:0x nightly. Measured 2026-08-24: 90 destination and cache volumes, 64.5 GiB restored, 124.4 GiB of Longhorn capacity with replicas. This is the same delete/recreate loop the 2026-07 Longhorn storage incident was traced to; 639a049d merged the split component back and recorded no rationale, so whether the nightly restore is an accepted cost of first-deploy safety or an unnoticed regression is written down nowhere. Treat as unresolved.

nodes.label: Pin the data, not the churn
nodes.norm_label: pin the data, not the churn
nodes.rationale: VOLSYNC_STORAGECLASS (default longhorn) controls the app's real data PVC; VOLSYNC_STAGING_STORAGECLASS (default longhorn-snapshot) the mover's throwaway staging clone and ${APP}-dst-dest; VOLSYNC_CACHE_SNAPSHOTCLASS (default longhorn-cache, misnamed — it is a storage class) the restic metadata cache. These were ONE variable until 2026-08-19, which is how the piece-12 Tier-1 migration put longhorn-critical on home-assistant's backup staging volume and cloned the full dataset onto three control-plane SATA disks at 3 replicas nightly. Exception: Tier 1 apps must point staging AND cache at longhorn-critical-snapshot/longhorn-critical-cache together, because Piece 12 Phase 5 restricts the default scratch classes to `bulk` and a Tier-1 app would have zero schedulable nodes while workers are powered down. Longhorn tag selectors are a hard filter with no preference order, so the choice is binary. Changing either staging variable is safe on a live app; changing VOLSYNC_STORAGECLASS on a bound PVC is not.

nodes.label: restic stale-lock unlock token
nodes.rationale: A mover that dies mid-prune leaves a restic lock that outlives the pod; every later source run then backs up fine and fails on forget/prune ('repository is already locked by PID ... on volsync-dst-...'). The failure is RETENTION, not backup — the snapshot is already saved, which is why it can run for days looking like broken backups while the data is fine (eight repositories on 2026-08-20, Tier-1 ones included). It is also an upgrade problem: tuppr's TalosUpgrade healthChecks gate on ReplicationSource Synchronizing == False, so stuck movers freeze node upgrades — the 2026-07 incident that left fluttershy and othalla cordoned for a week, and why talos.yaml carries a 15m timeout. The `unlock` field is a date-token: the operator copies it to status.restic.lastUnlocked and skips while they match, so it runs once per repository. Safe fleet-wide because the mover runs plain `restic unlock` (only stale locks; --remove-all is commented out in VolSync's mover-restic/entry.sh) and is a no-op on an unlocked repository. Bumped estate-wide on 2026-08-21 after a tuppr v1.36.3->v1.36.4 node roll killed in-flight movers mid-forget and stranded locks from SOURCE movers this time — either side can strand a lock.

nodes.label: pgloader Data-Only Load Job
nodes.rationale: Everything unusual is there because the alternative goes wrong: quote identifiers (or pgloader folds to lower case and finds no "Movies"), data only (or it builds its own schema over the app's), backoffLimit: 0 (a partially loaded database must never be loaded into twice), a digest-pinned amd64-only image, $(PGLOADER_TARGET) expanded by the kubelet not a shell, and the RWO config PVC attachable only because the app is scaled to zero. The target URI's password must be percent-encoded or a /, @, : or # produces a URI that parses wrong without complaining.

nodes.label: autobrrctl db:convert First-Party Converter
nodes.rationale: Runs the Postgres migration chain itself, so the target must be an EMPTY database — skip the schema-init and truncate steps. Foreign-key violations are dropped and reported rather than fatal, and are usually pre-existing orphans because SQLite does not enforce foreign keys by default. Everyone is logged out once (session store follows the driver and the converter skips the sessions table) and autobrr's own SQLite-only periodic backups become a no-op.

nodes.label: Boot-Budget Gate for Rotation Tranches
nodes.rationale: A rotation is a forced restart, and a restart is where latent startup fragility surfaces — added after tandoor crash-looped six times on a 2m40s collectstatic against a 40s liveness budget with no startup probe. Having no startup probe mattered far less than the ratio of boot to budget; the apps that broke had NEGATIVE margin. Measured spread is real: pinepods came back at 156s against a measured 144s.

nodes.label: Rotation Cutover Burst Tracks Connection Churn, Not Pool Size
nodes.norm_label: rotation cutover burst tracks connection churn, not pool size
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL does not terminate existing sessions when a role's password changes, so windmill's 49 live pooled connections kept working and it logged only 4 failures despite the prediction of the loudest cutover. Only NEW connection attempts in the rotate-then-propagate gap fail. Reconnect rate is the right thing to look at, not pool size. Propagation lag is ~3 minutes (ESO refreshInterval) and looks like failure while you wait.
nodes.source_location: What the cutover burst actually tracks (corrected)

nodes.label: Three Mechanisms That Make a Rotated Password Take Effect
nodes.norm_label: three mechanisms that make a rotated password take effect
nodes.rationale: Stakater Reloader (annotation on the WORKLOAD, not the pod template — windmill's chart puts it on the pod template, which is why the estate looked covered and was not), Helm valuesFrom re-render, and the ESO reloader Config CR. Windmill's password ends up as a plaintext literal in the Deployment pod spec because valuesFrom/targetPath injects it at render time.
nodes.source_location: Prerequisite: every consuming workload must see a rotated password

nodes.label: Rotation Cannot Be Switched Off
nodes.rationale: rotation_period is mandatory (min 5s), OpenBao has no skip_import_rotation, and creating a static role rotates the password immediately. openbao#284 is still open. Every app in a tranche becomes a rotating-credential app permanently, with reloader-driven restarts on the rotation cadence.

nodes.label: Derived bazarr --cast List
nodes.rationale: The wiki gives four --cast flags; at 1.6.0 the schema has eleven DateTime columns because the page predates the release that moved subtitles into new tables. Generate from the schema bazarr just built. The pg_depend exclusion and relkind='r' are both load-bearing — the obvious information_schema version also returns pg_stat_statements extension VIEWS living in public, and casting those breaks the run. Also: POSTGRES_ENABLED must be the literal string 'true', POSTGRES_URL does not work alone, and bazarr's own backup task branches on the config.yaml key not the env var.

nodes.label: Blanket TRUNCATE of the Seeded Schema
nodes.norm_label: blanket truncate of the seeded schema
nodes.rationale: Prowlarr's wiki page has no DELETE step at all, which reads as an omission rather than a claim it seeds nothing. Truncating every table in public is a strict superset, identical in effect since pgloader reloads immediately, and cannot drift as the schema changes. RESTART IDENTITY resets the sequences the seed rows consumed and CASCADE means tables need not be named in foreign-key order. TRUNCATE is not DROP.

nodes.label: flux resume Does Not Restore the Replica Count
nodes.norm_label: flux resume does not restore the replica count
nodes.rationale: The app-template chart only renders replicas when it is configured, and none of these apps configure it, so Helm does not own that field and the scale-to-zero survives the resume untouched. `rollout status` then reports 'successfully rolled out' against zero replicas and you will believe the app is up. Verified on prowlarr, where exactly that happened.

nodes.label: Generic pg_get_serial_sequence Fix
nodes.rationale: The wiki's per-app setval lists pass NULL on an empty table, skip a value on every table (is_called defaults true), and drift — Sonarr's still reads Blacklist_Id_seq from Blocklist. Deriving every sequence from pg_get_serial_sequence cannot go stale. pgloader does reset sequences on its own, so this is belt-and-braces, but the failure it prevents is silent until the first insert.

nodes.label: Single-Schema (public) Drift Check
nodes.rationale: All eight apps emit unqualified DDL, so tables go wherever search_path resolves first. components/postgres declares only public and no role-named schema, so "$user" has nothing to resolve to. Not boilerplate for three of them: bazarr's 0124f9e278fb_ migration probes table_schema = 'public' and seerr's FixBlocklistIdDefault hard-codes public."blocklist_id_seq". A second row named after the app means the $user element has armed.

nodes.label: Suspending the HelmRelease Does Not Stop Reloader
nodes.norm_label: suspending the helmrelease does not stop reloader
nodes.rationale: Suspension stops Flux, not reloader, which patches the pod template the moment ${APP}-env first syncs — rolling the Deployment onto an EMPTY Postgres database past a suspended HelmRelease. Not hypothetical: on 2026-08-27 autobrr was the one app left running because it reuses its existing autobrr-oidc Secret, and it came up on an empty database and applied its own base schema. Scale-to-zero in the same breath is the only thing that closes it.
nodes.source_location: 4. Phase 1 — merge, and let the database and role land

nodes.label: Throwaway Schema-Init Pod with Different Labels
nodes.norm_label: throwaway schema-init pod with different labels
nodes.rationale: The wiki says run the app once against the empty databases; doing that with the real Deployment serves an empty library to Prowlarr's app sync, Pulsarr, Overseerr and anything else holding the API key. A bare Pod with deliberately DIFFERENT labels does not match the Service selector, and emptyDir for /config means it cannot find a SQLite file and has no choice but to build its schema in Postgres.
nodes.source_location: 5.2 Create the schema — in a throwaway pod, not the app

nodes.label: ralgar pgloader Build for the Overseerr Family
nodes.norm_label: ralgar pgloader build for the overseerr family
nodes.rationale: Both projects tell you to use ghcr.io/ralgar/pgloader:pr-1531 because stock releases mis-quote column identifiers on this schema — a community artifact from a patch that was never merged, so it is pinned to the OCI INDEX digest (which keeps kubectl doing platform selection) rather than the floating tag. DB_TYPE must be exactly 'postgres' (strict case-sensitive, no warning), and overriding the container command drops NODE_ENV=production so migrations silently never run. Keep the `migrations` table when truncating and expect pgloader to error on exactly that one table.

nodes.label: Startup Probe for Migration and Rotation Cold Boots
nodes.norm_label: startup probe for migration and rotation cold boots
nodes.rationale: All eight had ~110s of liveness budget and no startup probe. First boot against an empty Postgres database replays the entire migration chain, and every rotation forces a cold start — a kubelet kill mid-migration restarts the pod, which replays from the top, which gets killed again. A startup probe suspends liveness AND readiness until it passes; 60 x 10s buys ten minutes and costs nothing on a normal boot.
nodes.source_location: 2. What lands in git — The startup probe

nodes.label: Forward-Migrating a Stale SQLite Copy Before Loading
nodes.norm_label: forward-migrating a stale sqlite copy before loading
nodes.rationale: When the app was upgraded before the data was loaded, a data-only load does not just lose rows — it fails on renamed tables (jellyseerr blacklist -> blocklist). The fix is to migrate the SQLite COPY forward using the new image in SQLite mode. Four traps: the migrations land in the WAL so copy all three files; the image ignores SIGTERM and SIGKILL from kubectl exec; pkill -f matches its own shell; and opening the copy locally with sqlite3 checkpoints the WAL, which doubles as preparation.

nodes.label: agents Namespace Umbrella Kustomization
nodes.rationale: NOT a boundary: the operator runs rbac.scope: cluster, so an MCPServer in any namespace is reconciled. This directory holds the operator, its CRDs and the MCP servers with no more specific home. Nothing registers the directory anywhere — cluster-apps points Flux at ./kubernetes/apps with no kustomization of its own, so the controller autodetects every subdirectory carrying one. Adding this file IS the registration. It brings its own app-template OCIRepository copy because that repo is namespace-scoped.

nodes.label: toolhive-docs Flux Kustomization
nodes.rationale: dependsOn toolhive rather than the operator directly — that Kustomization already depends on the operator and is what creates the MCPExternalAuthConfig and MCPOIDCConfig this server references by name. wait: true is real work here rather than a formality: kstatus gates on observedGeneration catching up on the MCPServer, which the operator does set, so a wedged MCP server surfaces as a failed Kustomization instead of a green one.

nodes.label: toolhive-docs MCPServer
nodes.rationale: The first real consumer of the operator next door — an operator with no CR does nothing observable, so nothing would prove the install works. The operator builds a proxy-runner Deployment, a backend Deployment and an mcp-${APP}-proxy Service, which is the only routable surface in the namespace. No yaml-language-server schema line because neither CRDs-catalog nor kubernetes-schemas publishes toolhive.stacklok.dev.

nodes.label: toolhive-operator-crds HelmRelease
nodes.rationale: The 14 toolhive.stacklok.dev CRDs, split from the operator the way upstream ships them. The split is not cosmetic: it lets the operator be uninstalled, rolled back or re-scoped without reaching the MCPServer objects. rollback.force is FALSE unlike most releases here — a forced rollback deletes and recreates what it cannot patch, and deleting a CRD takes every MCPServer with it. crds.keep stamps helm.sh/resource-policy: keep, which is the only thing standing between an uninstall and a cascade delete since this chart renders CRDs from templates/ rather than crds/.

nodes.label: toolhive-operator-crds Flux Kustomization
nodes.rationale: deletionPolicy: Orphan, the same rule as the CNPG and Garage operators: never cascade-delete on a Kustomization ownership change, because deleting a CRD deletes every custom resource of that kind and, through ownerReferences, the Deployments and Services built from them. wait: true is load-bearing rather than routine — the operator dependsOn this, and without the wait it could roll out against unestablished CRDs and its manager cache would fail to start on a missing kind.

nodes.label: toolhive-operator-crds OCIRepository
nodes.rationale: No verify: block — the chart repository carries 41 cosign sig tags but none matches a chart digest, so a verify block would fail every pull rather than protect anything. The digest pin is the real protection: the tag can move, the digest cannot. flux.pinDigests is false in renovate.json5 so Renovate will never ADD a digest, but the flux manager does rewrite an existing ref.digest alongside ref.tag.

nodes.label: toolhive-operator HelmRelease
nodes.rationale: The chart renders SIX objects and none is a Service, Ingress or HTTPRoute — everything with an HTTP surface in this namespace is created by the operator at runtime from a CR, which is why the route and the authorization server live in ../toolhive. No image/toolhiveRunnerImage/vmcpImage overrides on purpose, so the OCIRepository tag is the single version to bump and the operator can never drift from the proxy-runner image it injects. No priorityClassName and no control-plane toleration: MCP servers are developer tooling, so during a Low Power window the operator and its proxy runners go Pending together, which is the correct outcome.

nodes.label: toolhive-operator Flux Kustomization
nodes.rationale: dependsOn toolhive-operator-crds, or the manager cache fails to start on an unknown kind and the Deployment crash-loops with an error that reads like an RBAC fault.

nodes.label: toolhive-operator OCIRepository
nodes.rationale: KEEP THIS TAG EQUAL TO THE CRD CHART'S. Upstream publishes the pair at one version and this chart's operator.image default is derived from it, so a bump here without the matching bump next door runs an operator whose controllers register kinds the installed definitions may not describe. Renovate raises them as two separate updates; merge them together. Same no-signature/digest-pin situation as the CRD chart.

nodes.label: toolhive-operator PodMonitor
nodes.rationale: A PodMonitor rather than a ServiceMonitor because the chart renders NO Service at all. The selector matches the chart's own selectorLabels, not this Kustomization's commonMetadata — commonMetadata lands on the HelmRelease, never on the pods Helm renders from it, and app.kubernetes.io/instance is the RELEASE name, which is why fullnameOverride is restated. The operator takes no --metrics-secure flag, so this is a plain scrape with no TLS and no bearer token.

nodes.label: Cert Secret Is Owned by the DatabaseRole
nodes.norm_label: cert secret is owned by the databaserole
nodes.rationale: issueClientCertificate sets a controller ownerReference and deleteOwnedCertSecret removes the Secret outright when clientCertificate.enabled goes false. Deleting or disabling the DatabaseRole garbage-collects OpenBao's only credential, so the role needs kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/prune: disabled.
nodes.source_location: Two hazards found while reading the controller

nodes.label: Phase 1a Prune Guard
nodes.rationale: Moving a resource between Flux Kustomizations leaves the old owner's inventory listing it. The generated ExternalSecrets use creationPolicy: Owner, so pruning one garbage-collects the Secret CNPG reads. target.deletionPolicy: Retain does NOT cover this — it governs the provider-side key vanishing, not the ExternalSecret being deleted. The estate has already lost PVCs to this class of event.

nodes.label: tmp emptyDir for the Read-Only Root Filesystem
nodes.norm_label: tmp emptydir for the read-only root filesystem
nodes.rationale: The operator runs MCP server pods with a read-only root filesystem and this image writes its search index under /tmp while answering a query, so without the emptyDir every tool call fails while the pod stays happily Running and Ready. `mcp` is the operator's fixed container name — a different name appends a second container instead of patching this one. trustProxyHeaders is safe only because the sole path in is the Gateway, which sets X-Forwarded-* itself.

nodes.label: Helm Revision Secret Size Ceiling for a 1.1MB CRD Chart
nodes.norm_label: helm revision secret size ceiling for a 1.1mb crd chart
nodes.rationale: Helm stores each retained revision as one Secret holding the gzipped chart AND the rendered manifest — ~450 KB per revision here against Kubernetes' 1 MB Secret ceiling. History is not the risk (three revisions is three separate Secrets); upstream growing the definitions is. A 'request entity too large' error on a sh.helm.release.v1.* Secret is this, not a cluster problem.

nodes.label: Forgejo Actions Canary Workflow
nodes.rationale: Proves the Actions runner is not merely Running but actually executing jobs, by pushing hourly into a Gatus external endpoint whose heartbeat fails if no push arrives. This file is the canonical copy; the one that executes lives inside Forgejo, which is manual state. Forgejo only schedules workflows on the repository's DEFAULT branch. A heartbeat that hangs is a heartbeat that pages, hence timeout-minutes: 5.

nodes.label: gitssh Gateway Listener on Port 22
nodes.rationale: The container still binds 2222 because the rootless image runs as uid 1000; only the Service, listener and advertised port are 22. Talos nodes run no sshd and this binds the Gateway LoadBalancer IP, so nothing collides. The tailnet grant forgejo-git-ssh is restricted to tag:apps and must never be folded back into default-apps-access, which also reaches tag:dockge and tag:dns where 22 is a real shell.
nodes.source_location: What the manifests already do — SSH

nodes.label: Offline Forgejo Actions Runner Registration
nodes.rationale: Offline registration so the credential is one we chose rather than pasted from the UI. The printed UUID is not random — it is the hex encoding of the token's first 16 characters, so re-running with the same first 16 and different last 24 ROTATES the secret in place instead of creating a second runner. replicas must stay 1: every replica would read the same registration secret and share one runner identity.

nodes.label: stacks/system Forgejo Bot Provisioning
nodes.rationale: Two grant mechanisms because Forgejo has two kinds of owner: an org `renovate` team with includesAllRepositories covers future repositories automatically, while user-owned repositories need one collaborator grant each and so lag by a stack run. Archived, mirror and fork repositories are skipped deliberately. The stack authenticates as the BREAK-GLASS ADMIN with username and password, not a token, because Forgejo's /users/{username}/tokens route is reqBasicOrRevProxyAuth — a token-authenticated request cannot mint a token at all. Rotating that admin password is a Forgejo operation followed by a bao kv put, in that order.

nodes.label: Forgejo celestia to equestria Cutover
nodes.rationale: A re-create, not a migration — the celestia instance holds no repositories. Lands in the existing `coder` namespace rather than a new one because that is already the Low Power keep-list namespace and already carries the local-user middleware and the app-template OCIRepository.

nodes.label: curl --connect-to Tailnet Egress Hop
nodes.rationale: Pods have no direct route to the tailnet, so --connect-to keeps Host and SNI intact (Traefik still routes, the Let's Encrypt certificate still validates) while the connection actually goes out through the dockge-as egress. GATUS_TOKEN is both the URL path segment and the bearer — that is Gatus's external-endpoint convention.

nodes.label: Pulumi vs external-dns Race on git.driscoll.tech
nodes.norm_label: pulumi vs external-dns race on git.driscoll.tech
nodes.rationale: stacks/home deletes the old celestia CNAME (DockgeLxc reads traefik router rule labels out of compose files) while external-dns tries to claim the same name under policy: sync with a txtOwnerId, so it will not adopt a record it does not own. It self-heals on retry; the trap is the window during which git.driscoll.tech still resolves to celestia where the OLD Forgejo is still running — it is entirely possible to log into the old instance and conclude the new one is broken.
nodes.source_location: 2. Merge, and watch two Pulumi stacks race external-dns

nodes.label: Deleting a Dockge Stack Directory Does Not Stop the Container
nodes.norm_label: deleting a dockge stack directory does not stop the container
nodes.rationale: Dockge's .ignore path removes /opt/stacks/<stack>/ and leaves the container running and orphaned, and restart: unless-stopped plus autoheal resurrect it indefinitely. Requires a manual `docker rm -f`. The old database is likewise orphaned because provision.sh only ever creates, never reaps.

nodes.label: Dedicated Single-Node Garage for Forgejo Objects
nodes.norm_label: dedicated single-node garage for forgejo objects
nodes.rationale: One [storage] STORAGE_TYPE = minio block backs all eight object subsystems. replication.factor: 1 because 3x replication in front of an app that cannot run two replicas is redundancy that can never be exercised; durability comes from longhorn-critical underneath. Bare git repositories are NOT among the eight — Forgejo always keeps those on disk, so the PVC is still what a restore rebuilds the forge from. Its RPC secret must never be shared with garage-system or a node from one cluster could join the other's mesh.
nodes.source_location: What the manifests already do — Object storage

nodes.label: Forgejo JWT_SECRET Length Failure Is Silent
nodes.norm_label: forgejo jwt_secret length failure is silent
nodes.rationale: [security] SECRET_KEY is free-form but [oauth2] JWT_SECRET must decode to exactly 32 bytes. Given 48, Forgejo logs one line and proceeds with a key it invented — and because the chart rebuilds app.ini from the environment on every boot, that key differs every restart, so Actions task tokens and OAuth2 tokens silently die with the pod. Verify with `logs -c configure-gitea | grep -i jwt_secret`; silence is success.

nodes.label: Pulumi-Written OIDC Credential Bootstrap Cycle
nodes.rationale: The pod crash-loops until pulumi/equestria (stacks/applications) resyncs, reads the ApplicationDefinition CR out of the live cluster, creates the authentik application and provider, and writes clusters/equestria/apps/forgejo/oidc. ESO picks it up within its 4m refresh — allow ~10 minutes end to end. This circularity is the mechanism, not a fault.

nodes.label: Runner Canary Bootstrap (manual state)
nodes.rationale: Forgejo exports no runner metric at all, so a runner that is up but no longer accepting jobs — revoked registration, wedged poller — looks healthy to both ForgejoRunnerDown and ForgejoRunnerFlapping. Only a job that is SUPPOSED to run can tell 'nobody pushed today' from 'the poller is wedged'. It covers its own disappearance: whatever destroys the data volume destroys the canary repo, so the heartbeat lapses. It is manual state — a VolSync restore brings it back only if the repository was in the snapshot.

nodes.label: Second Garage Bucket for Renovate Logs and Cache
nodes.norm_label: second garage bucket for renovate logs and cache
nodes.rationale: Deliberately a second bucket on the Forgejo Garage cluster, not a prefix in `forgejo` — that one is backed up nightly and everything here is rebuildable. Size tracks repository count, not run count, because both prefixes are keyed by identity and each run overwrites the last. The log store fails QUIETLY: a log-store failure does not fail the Renovate run it was recording.
nodes.source_location: Log storage and the repository cache

nodes.label: Missing oidcConfigRef Makes the MCP Proxy Fail Open
nodes.norm_label: missing oidcconfigref makes the mcp proxy fail open
nodes.rationale: authServerRef is the ISSUING side and oidcConfigRef the ACCEPTING side; they are not interchangeable. Without oidcConfigRef the proxy runs UNAUTHENTICATED, accepting every request that reaches its port under a synthetic local-user identity — it fails open, quietly, with a healthy-looking pod. The audience MUST be unique per MCP server to stop token replay, and deriving it from the public URL makes that automatic. resourceUrl must be the external URL or RFC 9728 discovery loops.

nodes.label: Flux Kustomization ${APP}-postgres-databases
nodes.rationale: A separate Flux Kustomization exists because a Flux Kustomization has exactly one spec.path, and a CNPG Database is namespace-scoped with spec.cluster.name as a local reference, so the object must land in the `database` namespace next to the Cluster. The app's own Kustomization cannot do it because targetNamespace is Kustomize's namespace transformer and overrides an explicitly-set metadata.namespace. Keeping it separate also means a broken extra-database manifest still leaves the app its own database, login role and credential. Depends on postgres-operator rather than the postgres cluster Kustomization to avoid the openbao/postgres cold-boot readiness cycle; wait:false for the same reason; deletionPolicy Orphan so an ownership change never cascade-deletes a database.

nodes.label: postgres/databases Component
nodes.rationale: components/postgres renders exactly ONE Database named after the app; some applications need a second (a log or cache database with a different retention/vacuum profile, or a vendor hard-coding two connection strings). Consumers are sonarr, radarr, lidarr, prowlarr (<app>-log). Before this component the options were all bad: grant the app superuser so it can CREATE DATABASE, create it by hand and leave it undeclared, or fold a second Database into ../database where every app would get one. Deliberately invisible to Pulumi rotation discovery (stacks/system/postgres-rotation.ts matches components/postgres by exact path suffix) because an extra database reuses the app's existing role and needs no static role.

nodes.label: Flux Kustomization ${APP}-postgres-roles
nodes.rationale: Renders <app-dir>/postgres-roles/ into the `database` namespace. A DatabaseRole is namespace-scoped with spec.cluster.name a local reference so it must land beside the Cluster, and the app's own Kustomization cannot put it there because targetNamespace overrides metadata.namespace. Separate from ${APP}-postgres because a Flux Kustomization has exactly one spec.path. The directory must NOT be listed in the app's own kustomization.yaml or the roles render a second time into the app's namespace.

nodes.label: postgres/roles Component
nodes.rationale: Some applications' migrations reference roles they do not create — grant targets, RLS principals, ownership handles — assuming the migration runs as something holding CREATEROLE, which app roles here deliberately are not (login:true and nothing else). Consumers: toolhive-registry (toolhive_registry_server) and windmill (windmill_user, windmill_admin). Before this component the options were: hand the app superuser for a single statement, grant CREATEROLE permanently, or create the roles by hand — which is what happened to windmill, and why its two roles existed in the cluster and in no manifest.

nodes.label: postgres/superuser Component
nodes.rationale: Opts an app's database role into PostgreSQL superuser. It is a component rather than a POSTGRES_SUPERUSER substitution because a boolean cannot travel through postBuild.substitute — that field is typed map[string]string, a bare false is rejected by the Kustomization CRD, and quoting it in source does not survive kustomize build. Works by patching the nested ${APP}-postgres Kustomization to carry its own spec.patches entry, which Flux then applies to the DatabaseRole: two levels of patch, one level of indirection each.

nodes.label: Flux Kustomization cluster-apps
nodes.rationale: Owns the entire ./kubernetes/apps apply set and depends on cluster-meta. Its blanket patch adds SOPS decryption and postBuild.substituteFrom (cluster-secrets, cluster-versions, shared-secrets) to every child Kustomization, which is why per-app substituteFrom lists are always dead.

nodes.label: Flux Kustomization cluster-meta
nodes.rationale: The Flux root's meta layer (./kubernetes/flux/meta), ported from equestria-cluster for piece 21 Phase B and made live at the Phase C root flip. prune was false across the flip so an incomplete tree would surface as drift rather than garbage collection; restored 2026-08-14 only after the flip settled, 16 -ref stubs were deleted by hand, cluster-apps re-owned all 155 children, and a dry run showed 401 rendered objects against 401 inventory entries with zero difference. targetNamespace is hardcoded flux-system because Renovate lookups require it.

nodes.label: driscoll.dev/backup-credentials annotation requirement
nodes.rationale: The postgres-backup CronJob enumerates Database resources in the `database` namespace and for each reads the credential Secret this annotation names, defaulting to `<database>-postgres` — which for an extra database does not exist. Without the annotation the nightly run fails on a Secret that was never going to be there, and one failed database exits the whole job non-zero, at 02:00. Replaces an older three-document pattern (Database + <db>-postgres-conn Secret + duplicate ExternalSecret) with one line where the database is declared.

nodes.label: Postgres component family never prunes
nodes.rationale: The nested ks is deletionPolicy: Orphan and each Database carries databaseReclaimPolicy: retain plus kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/prune: disabled, so removing a file leaves the live database alone. `ensure: absent` DROPS the database and everything in it and is not a synonym for deleting the manifest. CNPG also will not recreate a database that disappears underneath it — it gates on observedGeneration == generation and no-ops even with ensure: present; force a reconcile by toggling spec.allowConnections.

nodes.label: Extra databases use only the public schema
nodes.norm_label: extra databases use only the public schema
nodes.rationale: A schema named after the role arms the dormant `$user` element of the default search_path and shadows public, splitting the app's data across two schemas. Extra databases therefore declare only `public`, owned by the app's own login role.

nodes.label: DatabaseRole adopts and forces every attribute
nodes.norm_label: databaserole adopts and forces every attribute
nodes.rationale: A DatabaseRole adopts an existing role and forces EVERY attribute to match the manifest, including omitted ones. Because these roles are frequently created by hand before being declared, read the live role first (pg_roles and pg_auth_members) and match it exactly. windmill_admin carries BYPASSRLS and is a member of windmill_user; declaring it without either silently strips a privilege the application's row security depends on.

nodes.label: POSTGRES_APP_PATH anchor idiom
nodes.rationale: A Flux Kustomization's spec.path is repo-root-relative and a component rendered into an app's build has no idea where that build came from — kustomize does not expose it. ${APP} is not enough because an app's directory is not derivable from its name (windmill under equestria/home, toolhive-registry under agents). So the app hands its own path down via `path: &path ...` / `POSTGRES_APP_PATH: *path`, written once so a moved app cannot end up with a stale path. postBuild substitution is textual over the whole rendered output, so it reaches spec.path like any other field. Forgetting the variable renders a bare `/postgres-roles` and fails with path-not-found — deliberate, so opting in without wiring the path says so. The same variable is read by the databases sibling, so an app using both passes it once.

nodes.label: JSON6902 append instead of strategic merge on spec.patches
nodes.norm_label: json6902 append instead of strategic merge on spec.patches
nodes.rationale: A Flux Kustomization is a CRD with no Go schema, so kustomize applies a JSON merge patch where a list REPLACES rather than merges — two sibling components each setting spec.patches meant the second silently won. A JSON6902 `op: add` to `/spec/patches/-` appends and composes. The target is scoped by the name regex `.*-postgres$` so it cannot reach a Flux Kustomization emitted by another component of the same app.

nodes.label: cluster-versions three-site coupling
nodes.rationale: cluster-versions is generated by components/common's configMapGenerator from a repo-root versions.env. Three sites must change together: versions.env, the generator plus both substituteFrom lists in components/common, and the entry in this root patch. substituteFrom is not optional by default, so a reference without a generator fails EVERY child Kustomization with 'ConfigMap/cluster-versions not found', while a generator without references silently substitutes nothing. It could not simply be dropped because the versions feed tuppr's Talos and Kubernetes upgrades — those CRs currently hold literal versions with their own renovate annotations, so nothing would break immediately, but removing the mechanism would foreclose collapsing that duplication onto one source of truth.

nodes.norm_label: gatus core config (storage, alerting, ui, web)
nodes.rationale: SQLite at /data/data.db with caching, concurrency 2, web port 9595. Defines the pushover default-alert every endpoint file inherits.

nodes.label: Gatus external-endpoint: Forgejo Actions canary
nodes.rationale: 3h heartbeat tolerating two missed runs of an hourly (17 * * * *) scheduled workflow — enough to ride out a node move, a Low Power window or a cold image pull, short enough to catch a wedged runner the same morning.

nodes.label: Gatus external-endpoint: openbao nightly-dump
nodes.rationale: Nightly at 03:00; 26h heartbeat interval so one missed dump goes red.

nodes.label: Gatus external-endpoint: openbao restore-test
nodes.rationale: Monthly on the 1st at 05:00; 792h (33 day) heartbeat covers a 31-day month plus one retry window. Past that the backup is formally untrusted per RUNBOOK Scenario D and someone should hear about it daily.

nodes.label: Gatus merged-directory config model
nodes.rationale: GATUS_CONFIG_PATH points at a directory; every YAML inside is merged into a single effective config. This is what lets Pulumi-generated endpoints and hand-written in-repo endpoint files coexist without either owning the whole file.

nodes.label: Pushover alerting provider
nodes.rationale: Credentials come from OpenBao via vals-style ref+openbao:// references to secrets/third-party-tokens/pushover/gatus. failure-threshold 4 / success-threshold 2 by default; individual heartbeat endpoints override to 1/1 because a lapsed heartbeat is already a multi-hour signal.

nodes.label: toGatusKey(group, name) token convention
nodes.rationale: External-endpoint push tokens are derived from group and name by toGatusKey in home-operations/components/helpers.ts (e.g. openbao-break-glass_nightly-dump, forgejo-actions_canary). Hand-written endpoint files must follow the same derivation so they are indistinguishable from the Pulumi-generated ones and reporters can compute the token.

nodes.label: Dropped gatus scrape job
nodes.rationale: The gatus job was deleted rather than migrated: it targeted gatus:8080 but the container is named uptime and listens on 9595, and Gatus only serves /metrics when metrics: true is set (it is not). Reviving it would have added a permanently-down target; enabling Gatus metrics is a separate piece of work.

nodes.label: Gatus /config mount must not be :ro
nodes.rationale: Gatus merges every YAML in GATUS_CONFIG_PATH into one config, so Pulumi-written endpoint files and in-repo static files must share a directory, the static ones layered as individual file mounts. runc has to CREATE a mountpoint inside the parent for any layered file that does not already exist, and on a :ro parent that create fails with 'make mountpoint: read-only file system' before the container process starts. default.yaml only escaped it via a stale 0-byte twin from June; openbao-break-glass.yaml had no twin and took the whole uptime stack down. The individual file mounts stay :ro — that is where read-only belongs.

nodes.label: Dead-man's switch for CI liveness
nodes.rationale: The Forgejo Actions runner is only observable WHILE FAILING: the ForgejoRunnerDown and ForgejoRunnerFlapping PrometheusRules watch the pod, and Forgejo exports no runner metric at all (modules/metrics/collector.go, gitea_ namespace, 28 series, none about runners). A pod that is Running, Ready, registered and no longer accepting jobs is indistinguishable from an idle CI system — a revoked registration, a wedged poller and an expired token all look identical. Only a job that is SUPPOSED to run separates idle from broken. Bonus coverage: the canary lives inside Forgejo as a repo+workflow, so anything that destroys Forgejo's data volume destroys it and the silence alerts — the 2026-08-24 volume loss passed unnoticed for exactly this reason.

nodes.label: Heartbeat silence as an enforceable failure
nodes.norm_label: heartbeat silence as an enforceable failure
nodes.rationale: The openbao-replica cronjobs POST success/failure through the dockge-as egress. Two loud failure modes: success=false turns the endpoint red immediately, and reporting nothing at all lapses the heartbeat interval and turns it red anyway. Silence is the dangerous one — RUNBOOK Scenario D declares a backup that has not proven itself in over a month UNTRUSTED, and these heartbeats are what make that statement enforceable rather than aspirational.

nodes.label: hermes (NousResearch agent runtime) container
nodes.rationale: Digest-pinned upstream multi-arch image (published by .github/workflows/docker.yml's publish+merge jobs), not the local `build: .` upstream compose uses. Tags are CalVer and inconsistently shaped (v2026.7.30 vs v2026.7.7.2), so a `versioning: loose` Renovate package rule is required or four-component releases are silently skipped.

nodes.label: homelable-backend container
nodes.rationale: No traefik labels and no published ports — reachable only through the frontend's nginx proxy. cap_drop ALL then re-add only NET_RAW, which is what the ICMP discovery sweep and `nmap -sS` actually use; strictly tighter than upstream, which only adds NET_RAW (a no-op, already in Docker's default set) and keeps the other ~13 defaults. SQLite at /app/data/homelab.db is the hand-curated canvas and is not reproducible from git.

nodes.label: homelable frontend container
nodes.rationale: On two networks, so traefik.docker.network is set explicitly to dockge_default so Traefik never dials the stack-private one. Native OIDC (AUTH_MODE=oidc) means no authentik forward-auth middleware, the same pattern as docker/celestia/pdm.

nodes.label: Native OIDC instead of authentik forward-auth
nodes.norm_label: native oidc instead of authentik forward-auth
nodes.rationale: Estate pattern: when an app ships its own OIDC client (hermes' bundled dashboard_auth/self_hosted provider, homelable's AUTH_MODE=oidc, pdm), it registers a confidential authentik oauth2 client in definition.yaml and gets NO forward-auth middleware on its Traefik router. Forward-auth is reserved for apps with no native OIDC.

nodes.label: ApplicationDefinition: Homelable
nodes.rationale: admins-only because the app renders a complete map of the network. Three layered gatus checks: the SPA shell (nginx serves it regardless of session, so a plain 200 is the right frontend signal), an API check on /api/v1/health which has no auth dependency and is nginx-proxied so it covers frontend -> nginx -> backend in one probe, and the Live View Blocked regression alarm.

nodes.label: The container is the only containment boundary
nodes.norm_label: the container is the only containment boundary
nodes.rationale: Upstream SECURITY.md 2.2 states that nothing inside the agent process constitutes containment — not the approval gate, not output redaction, not any pattern scanner, not any tool allowlist. Only the OS boundary counts, so every hardening key in this compose (cap_drop ALL, no-new-privileges, no docker socket, no host bind mounts) is load-bearing rather than decorative. vault#117 must be read before loosening any of it.

nodes.label: HERMES_UID/GID instead of a `user:` key
nodes.rationale: The image starts as root, remaps its internal hermes user via usermod/groupmod in the s6 stage2 hook, chowns /opt/data, then drops services with s6-setuidgid. docker/main-wrapper.sh and docker/stage2-hook.sh both hard-fail on `docker run --user <uid>` because bootstrap needs root and /opt/hermes is root-owned. A `user:` key would also make DockgeLxc (components/DockgeLxc.ts) chown the stack dir to a UID the container refuses to start as.

nodes.label: Six-capability minimum for the s6 bootstrap
nodes.norm_label: six-capability minimum for the s6 bootstrap
nodes.rationale: cap_drop ALL then re-add exactly six, verified empirically against this digest: CHOWN+DAC_OVERRIDE+FOWNER for the stage2 chown of /opt/data and the usermod/groupmod rewrites of /etc/passwd and /etc/group; SETUID+SETGID for s6-setuidgid dropping each supervised service from root; KILL for s6-supervise signalling its now-non-root children. no-new-privileges:true additionally stops any setuid binary in the image being a path back up.

nodes.label: /opt/stacks-data mount qualifies the stack for backup
nodes.norm_label: /opt/stacks-data mount qualifies the stack for backup
nodes.rationale: /opt/data is the single source of truth for all Hermes state (config, .env, sessions, memories, skills, cron jobs, hooks, logs, workspace). Upstream mounts ~/.hermes, which would sit outside the stack's backrest plan and silently not be backed up. stacks/backups/index.ts gives every stack whose compose references `stacks-data` its own plan whose pre-sync pulls exactly that directory — so the mount path is what creates the backup, and moving state elsewhere deletes the plan with it.

nodes.label: config.seed.yaml is a seed, not a bind mount
nodes.norm_label: config.seed.yaml is a seed, not a bind mount
nodes.rationale: On first boot the image seeds /opt/data/config.yaml from its 89KB example, which enables a very broad default toolset — and everything that matters for containment lives in config.yaml rather than env vars, so hardening must be in place BEFORE first start. init.sh copies this file only when no config.yaml exists; after that Hermes owns a live self-modifying file (hermes model, the dashboard settings tab, and hermes update's migrations all write to it). Editing this file does not change a running deployment; change it in the dashboard or via `hermes config set` and mirror it here so a rebuilt host comes back the same.

nodes.label: terminal.backend: local (whole-process wrapping)
nodes.rationale: 'local' runs tool commands inside this container as the unprivileged hermes user. Upstream calls this whole-process wrapping (SECURITY.md 2.2) and it is the supported way to contain everything — shell, code execution, MCP subprocesses, plugins, hooks, skill loading. The alternative, terminal-backend isolation, only confines what goes through the shell and would additionally require handing this container a docker socket. cwd is pinned to /opt/data/workspace so tool commands do not start next to sessions/, memories/ and .env.

nodes.label: Stack-private `backend` network alias
nodes.rationale: The frontend image bakes `proxy_pass http://backend:8000` into upstream's docker/nginx.conf, so the backend must answer to the bare name `backend`. That alias is scoped to the stack-private `homelable` network on purpose — claiming a name that generic on the host-wide dockge_default would collide with any other stack that ever adds a `backend` service.

nodes.label: Client Certificate CN Comes from DatabaseRole spec.name
nodes.norm_label: client certificate cn comes from databaserole spec.name
nodes.rationale: The Secret is named <metadata.name>-client-cert, but issueClientCertificate calls generateCertificateFromCA with role.Spec.Name. PostgreSQL cert auth maps CN onto the role name, so spec.name is the field that has to be right.

nodes.label: baoadmin — Certificate-Only Superuser Rotation Identity
nodes.rationale: No passwordSecret, no disablePassword — the certificate is the only way in from the moment the role exists, so there is no bootstrap password and no rotate-root ceremony. Superuser is not a choice: PG16+ restricts CREATEROLE password changes to ADMIN OPTION holders and CNPG's inRoles issues a plain GRANT, so a least-privilege rotator is unreachable declaratively. Mitigated by keeping `postgres` sops-backed and outside OpenBao's reach as break-glass. Separate Secret and separate mount (/etc/pg-admin-certs) from the storage cert so a superuser key is never one sslcert= typo away.

nodes.label: Talos API CA Rotation
nodes.rationale: Talos has no CRL, so rotating the CA is the ONLY way to revoke a client certificate — issuing a replacement admin cert does not invalidate the old one. Written after a talosconfig carrying an os:admin cert and its unencrypted ED25519 key was committed to a public repo. --kubernetes=false is deliberate: a leaked talosconfig is a Talos-API credential with its own blast radius.

nodes.label: OpenBao Postgres Client-Certificate Credential
nodes.rationale: OpenBao stores its own state in the shared CNPG cluster, so its database credential is the one credential in the estate that cannot come from OpenBao. A CNPG-issued client certificate beats generating a password and pushing it into KV: nothing to store, it DELETES objects (openbao-postgres ExternalSecret, openbao-storage ExternalSecret, the sops password document) rather than adding them, and CNPG already authenticates streaming_replica this way.

nodes.label: ESO ClusterSecretStore Instead of Reflector for Cross-Namespace Certs
nodes.norm_label: eso clustersecretstore instead of reflector for cross-namespace certs
nodes.rationale: Reflector requires reflection-allowed annotation ON THE SOURCE, even in explicit reflects: mode. Both source Secrets (openbao-client-cert, postgres-ca) are created by the CNPG operator, not Flux, so nothing in git can annotate them. ClusterSecretStore/database reads the namespace directly and is already the path openbao-storage used.

nodes.label: hostssl Rule Inertness Property
nodes.rationale: pg_hba matches on connection type, so a hostssl rule cannot match a non-SSL connection. Adding `hostssl openbao openbao all cert` while the connection URL still says sslmode=disable changes nothing about the running system, which makes the cutover a one-line change with a database-free rollback. Proven live via pg_stat_ssl joined to pg_stat_activity: six openbao connections, ssl=f, no client DN.
nodes.source_location: The property that makes this safe

nodes.label: pgx Caches the Client Certificate at Process Start
nodes.norm_label: pgx caches the client certificate at process start
nodes.rationale: pgx builds the client certificate into tlsConfig.Certificates inside configTLS, which runs once during ParseConfig at sql.Open. A renewed certificate on disk is invisible to a running OpenBao process, so renewal must ride on a restart. This is the finding that forces a volume mount rather than any other delivery mechanism.

nodes.label: Reloader-Driven Certificate Renewal Path
nodes.rationale: Three hops: CNPG patches openbao-client-cert in `database`, ESO re-syncs it into kube-system on an hourly refresh, and only then does reloader see the change and roll the StatefulSet. reloader.stakater.com/auto belongs on the WORKLOAD only; it is meaningless on a Secret or ConfigMap.

nodes.label: Split-Brain on Postgres Restore
nodes.rationale: Restoring Postgres from Barman brings roles back with backup-time passwords while OpenBao holds snapshot-time ones, locking every app out. Recovery is a loop of `bao write -f database/rotate-role/<name>`. This is also why the postgres superuser stays in sops and outside OpenBao's reach.

nodes.label: Proving the Old Certificate Is Dead Is the Gate
nodes.norm_label: proving the old certificate is dead is the gate
nodes.rationale: A rotation you have not proven rejects the old certificate has not remediated anything — the gate is the old talosconfig failing, not step 2 completing. The leaked blob stays retrievable from public git history by SHA, which is harmless once the cert no longer authenticates; do not treat history rewriting as the fix and skip rotation.
nodes.source_location: 6. Confirm the leaked credential is dead

nodes.label: rotate-ca Does Not Update talsecret.sops.yaml
nodes.rationale: talosctl rotate-ca generates a fresh secrets bundle internally and cannot accept an existing one (siderolabs/talos#12816, --with-secrets not implemented). This cluster is talhelper-managed, so after a rotation talsecret.sops.yaml still holds the OLD CA and the next genconfig + apply-config pushes it back, undoing the rotation or leaving nodes split-trust. Updating the file is a required step, not cleanup.
nodes.source_location: The trap this estate has that the upstream docs do not cover

nodes.label: discoverPostgresApps() Repository Discovery
nodes.rationale: Globs kubernetes/apps/**/ks.yaml and PARSES YAML spec.components, matching the path exactly so sibling components are not double-counted — which is why it correctly excludes autobrr's commented-out line where a shell grep counts it. But it never checks whether a parent kustomization actually includes that ks.yaml, so commented-out apps still count. Take the app list from this function, never from grep.
nodes.source_location: The app list is discovered, not typed

nodes.label: components/postgres Kustomize Component
nodes.rationale: One line in an app's ks.yaml renders a DatabaseRole, a Database and a credential ExternalSecret, and is the same signal the Pulumi stack discovers to create the OpenBao static role. Both halves derive from one signal deliberately: a hand-maintained list in the stack could disagree with the repo, a discovered one cannot.
nodes.source_location: Phase 1b / How an app opts in

nodes.label: OpenBao database Secrets Engine (stacks/system)
nodes.rationale: Two switches meaning different things: ENGINE_ENABLED decides whether the mount exists (off until the pulumi policy is widened, because stacks/system publishes clusters/<key>/details that every other stack reads); ROTATION_TRANCHE decides which apps get a static role, and creating one rotates immediately with no opt-out. Certificate PATHS not inline PEM, so the baoadmin private key never enters Pulumi state or the Minio backend. database/creds/* is deliberately withheld so dynamic roles are a 403 rather than silent design drift.

nodes.label: components/postgres Update.cs Generator (retired)
nodes.rationale: 314 lines of C# that walked every ks.yaml and spliced results into three central files. It existed only because before CNPG 1.30 there was no per-role custom resource — roles could only be declared inline in Cluster.spec.managed.roles. That constraint is gone.

nodes.label: Media Stack SQLite to PostgreSQL Migration
nodes.norm_label: media stack sqlite to postgresql migration
nodes.rationale: Eight applications in two families onto the shared CNPG cluster. Most upstreams call the SQLite migration unsupported and mean it — the Servarr pages support only fresh installs and the Overseerr family routes through a community pgloader build from an unmerged PR — so the rollback is not a formality. Four more apps (kapowarr, mylar, sabnzbd, qbittorrent) were checked and have no relational database at all.

nodes.label: Component-Emitted ks Does Not Inherit components/common
nodes.norm_label: component-emitted ks does not inherit components/common
nodes.rationale: ks.yaml files are collected by the umbrella kustomization, which is where components/common applies its decryption + substituteFrom: cluster-secrets patch. A component-emitted nested ks is built from the app path, so both must be written into the component's ks.yaml explicitly or ${CLUSTER_DOMAIN} silently fails to resolve.

nodes.label: Group E — Disabled Apps Leave Their Databases Behind
nodes.norm_label: group e — disabled apps leave their databases behind
nodes.rationale: outline, retrom and strmgen were commented out of their parent kustomization so no Flux Kustomization managed them, yet their CNPG Database CRs survived because components/postgres sets deletionPolicy: Orphan on its nested Kustomization. Disabling an app in the repo therefore leaves its database behind, silently. Order matters when dropping: CRs first (databaseReclaimPolicy: retain), then DROP DATABASE, then DROP ROLE — reversed, the controller recreates the database underneath you.

nodes.label: Pulumi SecretsMount URN Re-Parenting Incident
nodes.rationale: Re-parenting the SecretsMount into a PostgresRotationComponent changed its URN, which Pulumi reads as a different resource: create new, delete old. The create failed on 'path is already in use', which was the lucky outcome — a success would have unmounted database/ and taken every static role with it. Never resolve this by unmounting to 'clear' the path. aliases: [{noParent: true}] did NOT work; only the full old URN string did.

nodes.label: Nested Flux Kustomization from a Component
nodes.norm_label: nested flux kustomization from a component
nodes.rationale: Flux's spec.targetNamespace uses Kustomize's namespace transformer, which OVERRIDES an explicitly-set metadata.namespace — verified with a two-document fixture. So a component rendered inside an app's build cannot put Database/DatabaseRole in the `database` namespace; it must emit a nested ${APP}-postgres Kustomization with targetNamespace: database. wait: false and dependsOn: postgres-operator (not the postgres cluster ks) avoid the OpenBao/CNPG readiness cycle.
nodes.source_location: Why the component needs a nested Flux Kustomization

nodes.label: Brand-New App Ordering Trap (SQLSTATE 42704)
nodes.rationale: Two constraints point opposite ways: a MIGRATED app needs the Kubernetes half before the Pulumi run (the reverse rotates a password the app cannot read); a BRAND-NEW app needs the PostgreSQL login role before the Pulumi run or stacks/system fails outright on `role "x" does not exist`. Pulumi reliably wins the race against Flux's cluster-apps interval. Not made self-healing deliberately: the check would need cluster state, and an app omitted from the tranche is DELETED not skipped, so a transient read failure would destroy a live app's static role. Loud-and-stuck is the better failure.

nodes.label: DatabaseRole Adoption Forces Every Attribute
nodes.rationale: Creating a DatabaseRole for an existing role ADOPTS it and the operator forces every attribute to match the manifest, including omitted ones. Omitting superuser on immich would silently demote it, which is why ${POSTGRES_SUPERUSER:=false} is a substitution.
